citeAs: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár (2015). Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context. arXiv:1405.0312v3 [cs.CV].
creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár (Cornell NYC Tech, Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago, Facebook AI Research, Microsoft Research, Brown University, California Institute of Technology, University of California at Irvine)
description: Microsoft Common Objects in COntext (MS COCO) is a large-scale dataset for object detection and instance segmentation containing 328,000 images of complex everyday scenes with common objects in their natural context. The dataset includes 91 object categories with 2.5 million labeled instances annotated with per-instance segmentation masks. Images were collected to emphasize non-iconic views and rich contextual relationships between objects.
name: Microsoft COCO (MS COCO)
rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 workers per image for category labeling and instance spotting; 1 worker per instance for segmentation (with 3–5 workers for verification); 5 caption descriptions per image.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Worker quality on category labeling was analyzed by comparing AMT workers to 7 expert workers (co-authors). Ground truth was computed using majority vote of experts. The union of 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than any individual expert. Worker recall saturates at around 9–10 AMT workers. It was estimated that over 99% of all object categories not later rejected as false positives are detected given 8 annotators. Workers below a precision/recall threshold had all their work rejected. For segmentation, workers who consistently produced poor segmentations had all their work discarded.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The annotation pipeline consisted of three primary stages: (1) Category Labeling — workers used a hierarchical approach grouping 91 categories into 11 super-categories; 8 workers labeled each image, dragging category icons onto instances; (2) Instance Spotting — workers placed a cross on each instance of a given category, with up to 10 instances per category per image, aided by priming from the previous stage; 8 workers labeled each image; (3) Instance Segmentation — workers segmented each object instance using a modified OpenSurfaces interface; workers were required to pass a training task per category before contributing. A verification step had 3–5 workers judge each segmentation; segmentations not receiving at least 4 of 5 favorable votes were discarded. Crowd labeling was used for images with more than 10 instances of a category.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was explicitly designed to reduce iconic-image bias by collecting non-iconic images from Flickr using pairwise object/scene category queries rather than single-category searches. The authors verified experimentally that models trained on MS COCO perform better on everyday scenes than those trained on prior datasets. The dataset focuses only on "thing" categories (not "stuff"), which is acknowledged as a limitation. The long-tail phenomenon in instance counts per category (seen in SUN) was mitigated by ensuring each category has a significant number of instances.
rai:dataCollection: Images were collected from Flickr by searching for pairs of object categories (e.g., "dog + car") and scene/object category pairs to obtain non-iconic images with rich contextual relationships. At most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window were downloaded. In rare cases where enough images could not be found, single-category searches were used with an explicit filtering stage to remove iconic images. The result is a collection of 328,000 images.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images sourced from Flickr, collected by searching for pairwise combinations of object categories and scene/object category pairs. The raw images are photographs uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords.
rai:dataLimitations: The 2014 release is limited to 80 of the 91 categories; 11 categories were omitted (hat, shoe, eyeglasses — too many instances; mirror, window, door, street sign — ambiguous and difficult to label; plate, desk — confusion with other categories; blender, hair brush — too few instances). The dataset only labels "thing" categories and not "stuff" categories (sky, street, grass), which could provide significant contextual information. Object-part categories (face, hands, wheels) are not included. For images with more than 10–15 instances of a category, remaining instances are grouped as "crowds" and not individually segmented.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: After 10–15 instances of a category were segmented in an image, remaining instances were marked as "crowds" using a single (possibly multi-part) segment. Areas marked as crowds are ignored during evaluation and do not affect a detector's score. The dataset was split into two roughly equal halves for release: the first half released in 2014 (82,783 train, 40,504 validation, 40,775 test images), with the second half planned for 2015.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed (detected using a near-duplicate detection method) and images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize near-duplicates across train/val/test splits. An AMT filtering task was used to remove invalid or iconic images from candidate sets. Workers were shown examples of iconic and non-iconic images to guide filtering.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: MS COCO was released in two halves: the first half in 2014 and the second half planned for 2015. The paper states "MS COCO will evolve and grow over time; up to date information is available online." Future annotations planned include "stuff" category labels, occlusion amounts, keypoints, scene types, attributes, and full sentence descriptions.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to drive advancement of object detection and segmentation algorithms for scene understanding. Funding for all crowd worker tasks was provided by Microsoft. The dataset is designed to enable learning of detailed object models capable of precise 2D localization, which has broad applications in computer vision and AI systems that interact with the physical world.
rai:dataUseCases: Object detection, instance segmentation, scene understanding, contextual reasoning between objects, precise 2D object localization, image captioning, and benchmarking object recognition algorithms. The dataset is intended to advance state-of-the-art in object recognition by placing it in the context of broader scene understanding.

null_reasons.rai:annotatorDemographics: No demographic information about AMT workers is provided in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: No explicit discussion of missing data handling in the collection process beyond filtering iconic images.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific timeframe or date range for data collection is mentioned in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol described; missing/rejected segmentations are discarded and re-queued rather than imputed.
null_reasons.rai:machineAnnotationTools: No ML/automated tools used in the annotation pipeline; all annotation was done by human crowd workers on AMT.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: No discussion of personal or sensitive information collection; dataset contains natural scene images from Flickr.
